newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke does not see inflation taking off.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke does not see inflation taking off.

text.p: UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said he did not believe inflation was likely to "take off" in Britain.
"We are now a low-inflation country and I'm going to keep it that way," he said in an interview with BBC Television.
"The more sensible the fiscal policy the government produces, the less pressure there is on interest rates."
The budget should give people confidence that fundamentals would remain sound and that Britain would carry on with sustained growth, low inflation and healthier public finances.
"That is what helps us keep interest rates down, lower than they would otherwise be," Clarke said.
Asked if he thought Britain was embarking on an economic boom which his budget had done little to control, he replied:
"No, I don't. I gave my solid reasons in the budget speech why I don't think inflation is about to take off. Commodity prices are very flat, earnings growth is restrained and sensible."
"What are called producer prices...are very low indeed. Producer input prices have reduced compared with 12 months ago," Clarke added.
The housing market was becoming healthy again but was not in a wild boom. "We don't have the conditions we had in the late 1980s."
Manufacturing was picking up but was not yet racing away.
"We do have very strong consumer demand but the kind of growth we have is not out of line with what I forecast, not out of line with what is sustainable without inflation building up."
